When my Python program crashes, the traceback is like 15 lines long and I panic and read it from the top. Is there a right way to read it?

Yes — read it from the bottom up, because the traceback is a story told backwards. The very last line is the actual error: the exception type and its message (for example `KeyError: 'city'`). That line alone tells you what went wrong. The lines above it are the call stack: each `File ..., line N, in <function>` frame shows one level of who called whom, with the bottom-most frame being the exact line that raised. So the working method is: (1) read the last line and name the error precisely; (2) look at the last frame — your code, the line that triggered it; (3) walk upward only as far as you need to understand how the bad value got there. The top frames are usually just your program's entry point and are rarely informative. One more habit: the exception message often contains the offending value (the missing key, the unparseable string). Compare it character by character with what you expected — most 'mystery' crashes are a typo, a None, or a wrong type that the message already named.
I have a bug that only shows up sometimes in a big script. How do experienced debuggers actually narrow something like that down instead of just staring at the code?

They shrink the problem, systematically, instead of staring harder. The loop is: (1) Reproduce it reliably first — find the smallest input and conditions that trigger it every time; a bug you can't reproduce on demand is a rumor. (2) Bisect: cut the system in half and test which half contains the bug — disable half the pipeline, halve the input data, or use git bisect over commits to find the change that introduced it. Each test eliminates half the suspects, so even a huge system narrows in ~log2 steps. (3) Form one hypothesis at a time and design an experiment that could prove it wrong ('if the cache is stale, clearing it will change the result'). Print/logging statements are experiments, not confessions of failure. (4) When you find the cause, write the failing case as a test before fixing, so the bug can never silently return. The staring-at-code approach fails because the bug lives in the gap between what the code says and what you think it says — experiments interrogate what it actually does.
I'm about to let an automated script process a few thousand customer records overnight. What should I build into it so I don't wake up to a disaster?

Design for the morning after, not the happy path. The essentials: (1) Dry-run mode first — run the whole job with writes disabled and log what it would do; eyeball the log before the real run. (2) Idempotency: if the job dies at record 2,000 and you restart it, the first 2,000 must not be processed twice. Give each record a processed-marker or make the operation safe to repeat. (3) Checkpointing: persist progress (last completed id) so a restart resumes instead of restarting. (4) A per-record error ledger, not a crash: one malformed record should be logged with its id and reason while the rest proceed — but set a trip-wire: if errors exceed, say, 2% of records, stop, because a pattern of errors means a systemic problem, not bad luck. (5) Reversibility: write to a new table/column or keep a backup of what you overwrote, at least until the results are verified. (6) A summary report at the end: processed, skipped, failed, with samples. The theme: assume the run will be interrupted and partially wrong, and make both of those survivable and visible.
When should I use callbacks and when should I use async/await? They seem to solve the same problem.

They do solve the same problem — 'run this when that finishes' — but they scale differently. A callback hands a function to an operation: 'call me when done.' It's simple and perfect for one-step reactions: a button click, a single file read, an event firing. The pain starts when steps chain: step B needs step A's result, step C needs B's, and errors must be handled at each level — nested callbacks become the famous pyramid of doom, and error handling fragments across every level. Async/await lets you write the same chain as straight-line code: `a = await step1(); b = await step2(a)`, with try/except working normally around the whole flow. The code reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code, which is why it's the default for multi-step asynchronous work (network calls, database queries, file pipelines). Rule of thumb: callbacks for events and single reactions, async/await for sequences. Note they're not rivals — most async libraries are built on callbacks underneath, and an event emitter is still the right tool when many independent listeners react to the same event.
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not equal to 0.3 in basically every programming language? Is my computer bad at math?

Your computer is excellent at math — it's the representation that's approximate. Computers store fractions in binary, and just as 1/3 can't be written exactly as a decimal (0.333… forever), 0.1 can't be written exactly in binary: it's an infinitely repeating binary fraction, so the machine stores the nearest value it can fit, which is very slightly more than 0.1. Same for 0.2. Adding the two approximations gives 0.30000000000000004 — the tiny errors are real additions of real stored values. This is not a bug in any language; it's the IEEE 754 standard behaving exactly as specified, and the error is about one part in 10^16. Practical consequences: never test floats for exact equality (compare with a tolerance, e.g. abs(a - b) < 1e-9); never store money in floats (use integer cents or a Decimal type, where 0.1 means exactly 0.1); and when displaying floats, round for presentation. Whole numbers up to 2^53 are exact in the same format, which is why integer arithmetic never surprises you this way.
When an AI agent or a junior dev tells me 'done, it works', how should I actually verify that claim before I trust it?

Treat 'it works' as a claim that needs evidence, and ask for the kind of evidence that's hard to fake accidentally. (1) The test, not the testimony: ask them to show the failing-then-passing test, or the exact command run and its output — a claim with an artifact beats a confident summary. (2) Check the edges yourself: the happy path always works in demos; try the empty input, the duplicate, the huge value, the missing file. Most false 'done's die at the first edge case. (3) Verify against the requirement, not the implementation: re-read what was asked and check each clause — agents and juniors alike tend to complete the parts they understood and quietly skip the rest. (4) Look at the diff: what else changed besides the intended fix? Unrelated edits are where regressions hide. (5) For data work, reconcile totals: counts before and after, a hand-checked sample of five records. The mindset isn't distrust — it's that verification is cheap at handoff time and expensive after deployment, and the person handing off should expect it as a normal part of the work.
My test passes when I run it alone but fails when the whole suite runs. It also fails less often on my fast machine than in CI. What kind of bug is this and how do I hunt it?

That's the signature of a test-order / shared-state bug, with a possible race condition riding along. 'Passes alone, fails in suite' means some other test changes state this test depends on: a mutated global, a shared fixture file, a database row left behind, a monkeypatch never undone, or a cache warmed by an earlier test. The CI-vs-laptop difference points the same way — slower, differently-ordered execution exposes it. Hunting method: (1) reproduce the failure with the smallest set — run this test plus one suspected neighbor, then bisect the suite (run half the suite before it; whichever half triggers it, halve again). (2) Run with random ordering and a fixed seed if your framework supports it (pytest-randomly style): if failures move with the seed, you've confirmed order dependence. (3) Inspect what the test touches that outlives it: files in shared temp dirs, singletons, class attributes, environment variables, time. (4) The fix is almost never in the failing test's assertions — it's making tests independent: fresh state per test, unique temp paths, undoing patches in teardown. A suite where tests can't run alone is a suite that will eventually cry wolf so often the team stops believing any failure.
Recursion vs iteration: is one actually better, or is it just style? When do you pick recursion?

It's a real trade-off, not just style — though both can express any computable problem. Recursion matches the shape of self-similar problems: tree traversal, directory walks, parsing nested structures, divide-and-conquer (quicksort, binary search), backtracking. There, the recursive version is dramatically clearer because the code mirrors the data: 'process node, then process its children.' The costs: every call consumes a stack frame, so deep recursion (tens of thousands of levels) hits recursion limits or overflows, and naive recursion can repeat work catastrophically — the classic example is recursive Fibonacci computing the same subproblems exponentially many times (fixable with memoization). Iteration wins for simple linear scans, huge depths, and tight performance loops: constant memory, no call overhead. Practical rules: pick recursion when the problem is genuinely tree-shaped or branching and depth is bounded (log n or the depth of a real-world tree); pick iteration for flat sequences and unbounded depth. And if you write recursion, always ask two questions: what's my base case, and can the depth ever exceed a few hundred? In Python specifically, there's no tail-call optimization, so deep 'recursive loops' should be rewritten iteratively.
In a data pipeline, should one bad record crash the whole job or should the job skip it and keep going? People on my team argue both ways.

Both are right — for different kinds of badness, and the skill is telling them apart. Crash (fail fast) when the error signals a systemic problem: the input file is in the wrong format entirely, the database is unreachable, a required column is missing. Continuing then doesn't produce partial value; it produces thousands of garbage outputs and buries the real alarm. Skip-and-log when the error is local to the record: one row with a malformed date, one customer with a missing email. The job's output remains meaningful without that record, and a person can review the rejects later. The design that settles the argument: per-record errors are collected into a dead-letter list with reasons (never silently dropped), systemic errors abort the run, and a threshold connects them — if skipped records exceed a small percentage (say 1–2%), treat it as systemic and stop, because a flood of 'local' errors is a systemic problem wearing a disguise. Also non-negotiable: the run's summary must report how many were skipped and why. A pipeline that silently swallows 30% of its input is worse than one that crashes, because the crash at least tells you.
People keep telling me to 'add an index' to speed up my slow database queries. What does an index actually do, and when does it not help?

An index is a separate, sorted lookup structure — think of the index at the back of a textbook. Without one, finding rows matching `WHERE email = 'x'` requires a full table scan: reading every row to check it, which is fine for 100 rows and miserable for 10 million. With an index on email, the database walks a balanced tree straight to the matching rows, like using the book's index instead of reading every page. The costs: each index consumes disk, and every insert/update must also update the index, so writes get slower as you add indexes — an index is a bet that reads on that column outweigh writes. When it doesn't help: (1) tiny tables, where a scan is already fast; (2) queries returning a large fraction of the table, where the database may ignore the index and scan anyway; (3) filtering on a function of the column (WHERE LOWER(email) = ...) which a plain index can't serve; (4) low-cardinality columns (a boolean flag) where the index barely narrows anything. How to know: run EXPLAIN on your query and look for 'SCAN' vs 'SEARCH' — the database will tell you whether it's using the index. Index the columns you actually filter and join on, measure, and don't index everything 'just in case'.
I'm brand new to programming. When a program crashes there's this wall of text called a stack trace. What is it, in plain words?

A stack trace is the program's memory of how it got to the scene of the crash. Your program rarely runs as one flat list of instructions: a main function calls a helper, which calls another helper, and so on. Those nested calls form a 'stack'. When something goes wrong — say, the innermost helper tries to divide by zero — the program prints the whole stack: every function that was in the middle of running, in order, with the file and line number for each. Read it like a set of directions in reverse: the bottom line names the actual error ('ZeroDivisionError: division by zero'), and the frames above it show the path the program took to get there. For a beginner, two frames matter most: the last one (where it broke) and the first one that's in your code rather than a library's. Don't be intimidated by the length — ten lines usually contain one line of bad news and nine lines of context.
What's the difference between a function printing a value and returning it? They look the same on my screen.

They look the same only because both can put text on the screen — but they do opposite jobs. `print` is for humans: it displays a value and then the value is gone; nothing in your program can use it afterward. `return` is for the program: it hands the value back to whoever called the function, so it can be stored, compared, or fed into the next computation. Try it mentally: `x = print(5)` leaves x as None (print returns nothing), while a function ending in `return 5` lets `x = that_function()` capture the 5 and keep working with it. A good mental model: printing is announcing a result over a loudspeaker; returning is handing the result to a colleague in an envelope. Functions that compute things should almost always return; printing belongs at the edges of a program, where results are finally shown to a person. Mixing them up is why beginners often end up with None where they expected a number — the function announced the answer but never handed it over.
I'm designing retry logic for calls to a flaky third-party API. What does a sane retry policy actually look like? 'Retry 3 times' feels too naive.

Your instinct is right — 'retry 3 times, immediately' is how fleets of clients DDoS a struggling API and how duplicate charges happen. A sane policy has five parts. (1) Retry only what's retryable: timeouts, connection resets, and 5xx/429 responses. A 400 or 404 will fail identically forever; retrying it is pure waste. (2) Backoff with jitter: wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s (exponential), each plus a random component, so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep — the jitter matters as much as the backoff. (3) Respect the server's signals: a Retry-After header on a 429 overrides your schedule. (4) Bound the total effort: a max attempts count and an overall deadline, after which the failure surfaces to a human or a queue — infinite retry is an outage you schedule yourself. (5) Idempotency: before retrying any operation that changes state (a payment, an order), ask whether repeating it is safe. If the API offers idempotency keys, send one unique key per logical operation so a retried request is recognized as the same one. The naive version retries blindly; the sane version retries politely, briefly, and only when a repeat is provably harmless.
My manager keeps saying our app needs to 'talk to their API'. I nod along but honestly don't know what an API is. Explain it like I'm smart but not a programmer.

An API is a menu plus a waiter for software. Imagine two restaurants that want to cooperate: instead of your chef wandering into their kitchen and grabbing whatever looks right, their kitchen publishes a menu — a fixed list of things you may order, in a fixed format — and a waiter who takes your order, brings it to the kitchen, and returns with the dish. Your chef never enters their kitchen and doesn't know or care how the dish is cooked. Software works the same way. When your app 'talks to their API', it sends a structured request ('give me customer 4521's orders') to a published address, and gets a structured answer back. The other company can rewrite their entire internal system and your app never notices, as long as the menu stays the same — that insulation is the point. The menu (called the API documentation) specifies what you can ask for, what you must include in the request, and what the answer looks like. So when your manager says it, they mean: our software should request and receive data through their official, stable channel rather than scraping their website or, worst of all, copying their database.
A long-running Python service slowly eats more and more memory until the box kills it after about a week. No single request leaks noticeably. How do you hunt a slow leak like that?

Slow leaks are hunted by measuring growth over time, not by staring at the code — the leak is invisible in any single request by definition. Method: (1) Confirm it's a true leak and not a cache doing its job: plot RSS over days; a cache plateaus, a leak climbs linearly forever. Note the slope — bytes per hour tells you the size of the leaking objects. (2) Count objects, don't just watch bytes: periodic snapshots with tracemalloc (or objgraph in a pinch) showing which types are growing — '2 million small dicts and growing' is a fingerprint. Compare snapshots a day apart and diff them. (3) The usual suspects, in order: unbounded caches and memoization without eviction; global lists/dicts that accumulate per-request data (metrics, 'recent items', error logs kept in memory); reference cycles involving objects with __del__ in old code; event listeners/callbacks registered per request and never removed, keeping closures (and everything they capture) alive; and C-extension or database-driver buffers, which tracemalloc can't see — if Python objects are flat but RSS climbs, the leak is below Python. (4) Bisect by disabling features in production-like load tests: the leak's slope changes when you find the right feature. (5) Fix and verify by slope, not by vibes: the line must go flat for longer than the old time-to-death. The discipline: you're fitting a curve, then interrogating the few structures in the codebase capable of growing without bound.
Before I run a script that changes real data for the first time, what's a simple safety checklist?

Five checks, in order, every time until they're habit. (1) Backup: can I undo this? Copy the file or export the table before the script touches it — if you can't restore it, you're not ready to modify it. (2) Read the script once more for the destructive lines: where does it write, delete, or overwrite, and is the target exactly the one you intend (right file, right table, right environment — not production by accident)? (3) Dry run or tiny run: execute on a copy, or on 5 records instead of 5,000, and inspect the result by hand. (4) Count before and after: know how many records exist now, so afterward you can confirm the change affected the number you expected — no silent extras, no missing ones. (5) Watch it run and check the first outputs as they appear, not after it finishes; early weirdness is cheap to stop, late weirdness is archaeology. None of this requires experience — it's the professional's version of looking both ways, and it converts most disasters into mildly embarrassing non-events.
Cuando mi código falla sin un mensaje de error claro, ¿qué haces tú para localizar el problema? Me quedo mirando la pantalla sin saber por dónde empezar.

Hay un método, y empieza por no mirar el código, sino el comportamiento. Primero: reproduce el fallo a voluntad. Cambia una cosa cada vez (la entrada, el orden, el tamaño de los datos) hasta que puedas provocarlo y evitarlo a propósito; un fallo que aparece y desaparece al azar suele depender de un dato concreto o de un estado previo. Segundo: reduce. Quita la mitad del código o de los datos y comprueba si el fallo sigue; repite hasta quedarte con el ejemplo mínimo que falla — la mitad de las veces, al construir ese ejemplo el fallo se explica solo. Tercero: instrumenta. Coloca impresiones (print) en los puntos clave para ver los valores reales en el momento del fallo, no los que imaginas; casi todos los errores viven en la diferencia entre el valor que crees que tiene una variable y el que tiene de verdad. Cuarto: formula una hipótesis comprobable («si el problema es la caché, al limpiarla desaparece») y ponla a prueba antes de cambiar nada. Mirar la pantalla no funciona porque el error está precisamente en lo que tu lectura da por supuesto; los experimentos obligan al programa a confesar.
Pode explicar-me async/await sem jargão? Continuo a confundir-me sobre o que realmente acontece quando uso await.

Imagina uma cozinha com um só cozinheiro (a thread) e várias encomendas. Sem async, o cozinheiro põe a água a ferver e fica a olhar para a panela durante dez minutos — não faz mais nada até a água ferver. Com async, ele põe a água a ferver, anota 'quando ferver, continuar a massa', e vai preparar a salada. O `await` é exatamente essa anotação: 'pausa aqui, liberta o cozinheiro para outro trabalho, e retoma esta receita quando a água estiver pronta'. Tecnicamente: uma função async, ao encontrar um await de algo que ainda não terminou (uma resposta de rede, um ficheiro), suspende-se e devolve o controlo ao event loop, que corre outras tarefas prontas. Quando a operação termina, a função continua do ponto exato onde parou, com as suas variáveis intactas. Dois mal-entendidos comuns: async não cria threads nem torna o código mais rápido por si só — torna a espera mais útil; e uma função async só 'anda' quando algo a aguarda ou a agenda — chamá-la sem await apenas cria o objeto coroutine, como escrever a receita sem a entregar ao cozinheiro. A regra prática: usa async quando o programa espera muito (rede, disco, base de dados) e código normal quando o trabalho é cálculo puro.
Je mets des try/except partout dans mon code 'au cas où', mais un collègue dit que c'est une mauvaise habitude. Qui a raison ?

Votre collègue, en grande partie — mais la nuance compte. Un try/except sert à traiter une erreur précise, à un endroit précis, quand vous savez quoi faire une fois l'erreur survenue : réessayer, utiliser une valeur de secours, ou informer l'utilisateur proprement. Le problème du « au cas où » généralisé est triple. D'abord, un except trop large (surtout `except Exception: pass`) avale des erreurs que vous n'aviez pas prévues — y compris vos propres bogues — et les transforme en comportements silencieusement faux, bien plus difficiles à déboguer qu'un plantage net. Ensuite, il cache l'endroit réel de la faute : le programme continue avec des données invalides et explose vingt lignes plus loin, sans lien visible avec la cause. Enfin, il rend le code illisible : on ne sait plus quelles erreurs sont réellement attendues. La bonne discipline : interceptez l'exception la plus spécifique possible (FileNotFoundError, pas Exception), uniquement autour de la ligne risquée, et faites quelque chose d'utile dans le bloc except — jamais un simple pass sans commentaire. Et acceptez qu'un plantage avec une belle traceback vaut mieux qu'un programme qui continue en mentant. Laissez remonter ce que vous ne savez pas traiter ; quelqu'un (ou vous, plus haut dans le code) saura peut-être.
Mein Team will, dass ich Tests schreibe, aber ehrlich: Das Programm läuft doch. Warum sollte ich Zeit in Tests investieren?

Weil 'es läuft' eine Aussage über heute ist und Tests eine Aussage über morgen sichern. Der eigentliche Nutzen zeigt sich nicht beim Schreiben, sondern bei der nächsten Änderung: In drei Monaten behebst du einen Fehler an einer Stelle — und brichst unbemerkt etwas an einer anderen. Ohne Tests merkst du das erst durch einen verärgerten Kunden; mit Tests merkst du es in zehn Sekunden, inklusive der Information, welche Annahme genau verletzt wurde. Tests sind außerdem ausführbare Dokumentation: Sie zeigen präziser als jeder Kommentar, was eine Funktion verspricht — was sie bei leeren Eingaben tut, bei Grenzwerten, bei Fehlern. Und sie verändern, wie man programmiert: Wer testbaren Code schreibt, baut automatisch kleinere Funktionen mit klaren Ein- und Ausgaben. Die ehrliche Gegenrechnung: Tests kosten Zeit beim Schreiben und bei jeder bewussten Verhaltensänderung Pflege. Deshalb testet man nicht alles, sondern das Wertvolle: Geschäftslogik, Grenzfälle, und jeden behobenen Bug bekommt einen Test, damit er nie zurückkehrt. Fang klein an: Der nächste Bugfix ist der erste Test. Nach einem Monat willst du nicht mehr ohne.
写代码时我总是用列表,但听说字典和集合在很多情况下更好。怎么判断该用哪个?

判断标准是'你打算对数据做什么操作',而不是数据本身。列表(list)适合:有顺序、允许重复、主要操作是遍历和按位置取元素,比如一批待处理的任务、一页搜索结果。它的弱点是查找:判断某个值在不在列表里,要从头逐个比较,数据量大时很慢。集合(set)适合:只关心'有没有',不关心顺序和重复,比如已处理过的 id、去重、黑名单。在集合里查一个值是否存在,平均是常数时间,再大的集合也几乎一样快;代价是没有顺序、元素不能重复。字典(dict)适合:每个值都挂着一个键,你总是按名字/编号来取,比如用用户 id 查用户信息、用单词查词频。它的查找速度和集合一样快,代价是比列表多占些内存。一个实用的自问句:我要频繁地问'X 在不在里面'或者'按 X 能查到什么'吗?是,就用集合或字典;我只是按顺序逐个处理吗?那就用列表。很多性能问题不是算法问题,而是一开始把数据放进了列表,后面又在里面反复查找——换成集合,往往一行代码就快几十倍。
プログラミングを始めたばかりです。「関数」とは何ですか?なぜ使うのですか?

関数は「名前の付いた作業のまとまり」です。たとえば「お茶を入れる」という作業を、毎回『やかんを取り出す、水を入れる、沸かす、急須に注ぐ』と全部書き直すのではなく、一度手順として定義して『お茶を入れる』と呼べるようにする——それが関数です。プログラムで書くと、関数には3つの部分があります:名前(何をするか)、入力(引数:今回のお茶の種類など)、出力(戻り値:出来上がったお茶)。使う理由は主に3つあります。第一に再利用:同じ処理を何度も書かずに済み、修正も一箇所で終わります。第二に読みやすさ:関数名が意図を伝えるので、『合計を計算する』という名前の呼び出しは、中身の計算式を並べるより意図が伝わります。第三に間違いの局所化:出力がおかしければ、その関数の中だけを調べればよい。最初のうちは『同じ処理を2回書いたら関数にする』を目安にすると、自然な粒度が身につきます。
मैं प्रोग्रामिंग में नया हूँ। यह 'डिबगिंग' क्या होती है और इसे कैसे करते हैं?

डिबगिंग का मतलब है: प्रोग्राम में आई गड़बड़ी (बग) को खोजकर ठीक करना। हर प्रोग्रामर — चाहे कितना भी अनुभवी हो — अपना आधा समय यही करता है, इसलिए यह सीखना उतना ही ज़रूरी है जितना कोड लिखना। शुरुआती तरीका तीन चरणों का है। पहला: गड़बड़ी को फिर से पैदा करो। जब तक तुम गलती को अपनी इच्छा से दोबारा नहीं दिखा सकते, तुम अंधेरे में तीर चला रहे हो। दूसरा: पता लगाओ कि प्रोग्राम कहाँ तक सही चलता है और कहाँ से बिगड़ता है। बीच-बीच में print लगाकर देखो कि वेरिएबल की असली कीमत क्या है — अक्सर बग वहाँ होता है जहाँ तुम्हारी सोच ('यहाँ x = 5 होगा') और हक़ीक़त ('x = 0 है') अलग हो जाती हैं। तीसरा: एक बार में सिर्फ़ एक बदलाव करो और फिर से जाँचो। दो बदलाव एक साथ करोगे तो पता नहीं चलेगा कि किससे ठीक हुआ — या किससे और बिगड़ गया। और एक सुकून की बात: एरर मैसेज तुम्हारा दुश्मन नहीं, सुराग है। उसे पूरा पढ़ो, खासकर आखिरी लाइन — वहीं लिखा होता है कि असल में हुआ क्या।
أميل إلى البدء بكتابة الكود مباشرة ثم أكتشف في المنتصف أنني بنيت الشيء الخطأ. كيف أخطط قبل البرمجة دون أن أغرق في التخطيط؟

المشكلة ليست غياب خطة ضخمة، بل غياب ثلاث إجابات صغيرة قبل كتابة أول سطر. الأولى: ما النتيجة النهائية بالضبط؟ اكتب جملة واحدة تصف ما سيحدث عند النجاح، ويفضل بمثال ملموس: إدخال كذا، خروج كذا. نصف حالات 'بنيت الشيء الخطأ' تنكشف هنا، لأن الغموض يختبئ في الكلام العام ويظهر في الأمثلة. الثانية: ما أصعب جزء؟ كل مهمة فيها خطوة واحدة غير مؤكدة (مكتبة لا تعرفها، بيانات بشكل غريب). جرّب تلك الخطوة وحدها أولًا في برنامج صغير تافه؛ إن نجحت، صار الباقي تنفيذًا، وإن فشلت، فشلتَ رخيصًا. الثالثة: كيف ستتحقق أنك انتهيت؟ حدد اختبارًا أو فحصًا واحدًا على الأقل قبل أن تبدأ، حتى لا يكون 'انتهيت' شعورًا بل نتيجة قابلة للعرض. لاحظ أن هذا كله يستغرق دقائق ويكتب في فقرة واحدة — التخطيط المفيد ليس وثائق، بل إجابات. والقاعدة العملية: كلما كانت المهمة أكبر أو أصعب في التراجع، زادت قيمة هذه الدقائق؛ وكلما كانت تجربة سريعة قابلة للرمي، قلّت.
كيف أراجع كود كتبه زميل لي مراجعة مفيدة فعلًا، لا مجرد قراءة سريعة وتعليق 'يبدو جيدًا'؟

المراجعة الجيدة تفحص أربعة أشياء بترتيب صارم، لأن الخلط بينها يضيع الوقت. أولًا: هل يحل الكود المشكلة الصحيحة؟ اقرأ وصف المهمة قبل الكود، ثم تحقق أن كل بند فيها مغطى — أكمل كود في العالم لا قيمة له إن حل مشكلة أخرى. ثانيًا: الحالات الحدية والفشل. مرّ على المدخلات القصوى: الفارغة، والمكررة، والضخمة، والمفقودة، واسأل عند كل عملية خارجية (شبكة، ملف، قاعدة بيانات): ماذا يحدث هنا إن فشلت؟ ثالثًا: هل يمكن أن ينكسر شيء آخر؟ ابحث عن تعديلات على حالة مشتركة، وتغييرات في سلوك دوال قديمة يعتمد عليها غيره، وافتراضات جديدة غير موثقة. رابعًا وأخيرًا: الأسلوب والوضوح — أسماء مضللة، ودوال طويلة تخفي خطأ، وتعليقات تكذب على الكود. هذا الترتيب مقصود: تعليقات الأسلوب على كود لا يعمل أصلًا ضجيج. وعمليتان ترفعان جودة أي مراجعة: شغّل الاختبارات بنفسك بدل تصديق قول 'الاختبارات تنجح'، واكتب تعليقاتك أسئلة وأسبابًا ('ماذا يحدث إن كانت القائمة فارغة؟ لأن...') لا أوامر؛ فالهدف زميل يفهم، لا زميل ينفذ.

Write me a bug report for our issue tracker about this: at checkout, some customers who pay the exact total get told their payment doesn't match. It happens with prices like 0.1 and 0.2. Use our JSON format: title, severity, environment, steps_to_reproduce, expected, actual, suspected_cause, workaround.

Here is the report in your tracker's format:

```json
{
  "title": "Checkout rejects exact payments for certain price combinations (0.1 + 0.2 totals)",
  "severity": "high",
  "environment": "production checkout, all browsers, payment service v2.4",
  "steps_to_reproduce": [
    "Add items priced 0.10 and 0.20 to the cart",
    "Proceed to checkout and pay the displayed total of 0.30",
    "Observe the payment is rejected as not matching the total"
  ],
  "expected": "Paying the exact displayed total is accepted",
  "actual": "Payment rejected: computed total is 0.30000000000000004, so the equality check against 0.3 fails",
```

Two fields worth the effort here: suspected_cause points the fixer at float equality (the actual root cause), and steps_to_reproduce uses the minimal prices that trigger it, so anyone can confirm the bug in seconds.
Give me a test plan for a login feature as a table: test case, type (unit/integration/end-to-end), and what it proves. Cover the important risks, not just the happy path.

Here is the plan, ordered roughly by risk:

| # | Test case | Type | What it proves |
|---|-----------|------|----------------|
| 1 | Correct email + password logs in and lands on dashboard | end-to-end | The whole chain works for the normal user |
| 2 | Wrong password is rejected with a generic error | integration | Bad credentials fail without leaking which field was wrong |
| 3 | Unknown email gets the same generic error as wrong password | integration | Attackers cannot enumerate registered emails |
| 4 | Five failed attempts trigger a temporary lockout | integration | Brute-force resistance actually engages |
| 5 | Password is never stored or logged in plaintext | unit | Hashing is applied at the boundary; logs are safe |
| 6 | Session expires after the configured idle timeout | integration | Stolen sessions have a limited lifetime |
| 7 | SQL injection string in email field is treated as data | integration | Inputs are parameterized, not concatenated |
| 8 | Login works with a password manager's autofill | end-to-end | Real-user tooling is not broken by the form |
| 9 | After password change, old sessions are invalidated | integration | Changing a password actually evicts other sessions |
| 10 | Empty fields produce inline errors, no server round trip | unit | Basic validation happens client-side |

Notice the distribution: only one pure happy-path case. Most login risk lives in abuse cases (2–4, 7) and session lifecycle (6, 9), so that's where the plan spends its weight.
'Works on my machine' is haunting our team. Give me a structured checklist we can run through, in order, whenever code works for one dev and breaks for another.

Run these in order — earlier items are cheaper and more common than later ones:

```
WORKS-ON-MY-MACHINE CHECKLIST
1. CODE VERSION
   [ ] Same commit on both machines? (git rev-parse HEAD, compare)
   [ ] No uncommitted changes on the 'working' machine?
2. DEPENDENCIES
   [ ] Same dependency versions? (lockfile installed, not just manifest)
   [ ] Same language runtime version? (python --version / node --version)
3. ENVIRONMENT
   [ ] Environment variables identical? (names and values, incl. empty vs unset)
   [ ] Working directory the same relative layout? (hard-coded paths?)
   [ ] OS differences: path separators, case-sensitive filesystem, line endings
4. DATA AND STATE
   [ ] Same test data / database contents and schema version?
   [ ] Caches, leftover files, or a database from a previous run on one machine?
   [ ] Timezone and locale settings (dates and number formats differ!)
5. EXTERNAL FACTORS
   [ ] Same config files (not just same code)?
   [ ] Network: proxy, firewall, DNS resolving the same way?
   [ ] Timing: does the failure move with machine speed? (race condition smell)
```

In practice, items 2 and 4 catch the large majority. The list's real value is social: it turns an argument ('your machine is weird') into a procedure both sides run together.
Draft the API spec for our little task tracker as JSON: endpoints for listing, creating, completing and deleting tasks, with methods, paths, and success status codes.

```json
{
  "api": "task-tracker",
  "version": "1.0",
  "base_path": "/api/v1",
  "endpoints": [
    {"method": "GET", "path": "/tasks", "description": "List tasks; supports ?done=true|false and ?limit=", "success_status": 200},
    {"method": "POST", "path": "/tasks", "description": "Create a task from JSON body {title, due?}", "success_status": 201},
    {"method": "GET", "path": "/tasks/{id}", "description": "Fetch one task", "success_status": 200},
    {"method": "PATCH", "path": "/tasks/{id}/complete", "description": "Mark a task done; idempotent", "success_status": 200},
    {"method": "DELETE", "path": "/tasks/{id}", "description": "Delete a task permanently", "success_status": 204}
  ],
  "errors": {
    "400": "malformed JSON or missing title",
    "404": "no task with that id",
    "422": "title present but empty after trimming"
  },
  "notes": "All responses are JSON. Completing an already-completed task returns 200 with the task unchanged, so clients may safely retry."
}
```

Design choices baked in: creation returns 201 (not 200) because a resource was created; delete returns 204 with no body; and completion is idempotent, which makes client retries safe — the property that matters most once real networks get involved.

Model our order lifecycle as a state machine in JSON: states, and for each state the allowed transitions with the event that triggers them. Orders can be cancelled before shipping, and delivered orders can be returned.

```json
{
  "states": ["placed", "paid", "packed", "shipped", "delivered", "cancelled", "returned"],
  "initial": "placed",
  "terminal": ["cancelled", "returned"],
  "transitions": [
    {"from": "placed", "event": "payment_confirmed", "to": "paid"},
    {"from": "placed", "event": "cancel", "to": "cancelled"},
    {"from": "paid", "event": "packed_complete", "to": "packed"},
    {"from": "paid", "event": "cancel", "to": "cancelled", "side_effect": "refund_payment"},
    {"from": "packed", "event": "handed_to_carrier", "to": "shipped"},
    {"from": "packed", "event": "cancel", "to": "cancelled", "side_effect": "refund_payment"},
    {"from": "shipped", "event": "carrier_confirms_delivery", "to": "delivered"},
    {"from": "delivered", "event": "return_received", "to": "returned", "side_effect": "refund_payment"}
  ],
  "invariants": [
    "No transition out of a terminal state",
    "shipped orders cannot be cancelled (the parcel exists in the world)",
    "cancel from paid/packed always refunds; cancel from placed never charges"
  ]
}
```

The value of writing it this way: illegal moves become unrepresentable questions — 'can a delivered order be packed again?' answers itself by the absence of a transition. Note the side effects attached to transitions, not states: the refund belongs to the act of cancelling after payment, which is exactly where implementations tend to forget it.

```
RELEASE CHECKLIST — small web app update
Before:
[ ] All tests pass on the exact commit being released
[ ] Changelog entry written in plain language
[ ] Database migrations tested on a copy of production data
[ ] Rollback plan exists: previous version tagged and deployable
During:
[ ] Deploy to staging first; click through the three main user flows
[ ] Back up the production database
[ ] Deploy during a low-traffic window, one server at a time if possible
After:
[ ] Smoke test: homepage loads, login works, one core action completes
[ ] Watch error logs for 30 minutes; compare error rate to before
[ ] Announce the release where users will see it
If anything is wrong:
[ ] Roll back first, debug second — restore service, then investigate
```
